question: Beekeeping is a pillar of the rural economy and biodiversity in Greece and Europe. However, this sector is faced with enormous challenges that are a direct threat to its viability. Climate change, prolonged droughts, rising temperatures, fires and constant influxes of African dust have significantly affected the availability of pollen and nectar, hindering the survival of bees.

Furthermore, the import of adulterated honey, unfair market practices and rocketing production costs are making the beekeeper’s profession financially unviable, so that increasing numbers of producers are abandoning the sector. The support programme provided under the common agricultural policy is proving to be insufficient to cover current needs.
Beekeepers play a crucial role in protecting biodiversity and agriculture, and unless immediate and substantive measures are taken, the sector will reach a dead end. In view of this: 1.
What measures does the Commission intend to take to provide immediate support to beekeepers who are suffering the effects of adverse climate conditions and extreme economic pressures?

How does the Commission intend to reinforce the controls to combat adulteration and unlawful imports of low-quality honey, which are harmful to the reputation of local produce and are driving producers to despair?
Will the EU step up its policies on promoting a viable beekeeping industry and protecting biodiversity, for example by introducing an annual pollination subsidy per hive?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.1.2025) The Commission is committed to help address the challenges faced by the beekeeping sector through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and various policy initiatives to safeguard pollinators and their environment.

Under the national CAP Strategic Plans, beekeepers can benefit from apiculture support with an annual EU budget of EUR 60 million, which is at least doubled with national co-financing to support investments/actions to improve production and marketing, prevent damage caused by adverse climate and promote climate change adaptation practices.

The CAP also supports the adoption of bee-friendly farming practices including pesticide risk reductions or increasing floral resources in non-productive landscape features. Further exceptional emergency measures1 to support farmers were adopted by the Commission in October 2024.

As expressed in its replies to written questions E-000209/20242 and 000343/20243, the Commission adopted measures to address honey adulteration at EU level. EU import requirements were reinforced with an authenticity requirement for exporting countries4 and the import of honey is now only possible from listed establishments5.

In 2023, the Commission launched a project to harmonise analytical methods to better detect honey adulterants, while Directive (EU) 2024/14386 introduced mandatory indication of origin for honey blends and new provisions on traceability and authenticity. The promotion of a viable beekeeping sector and protection of biodiversity are key priorities for the Commission.

While the introduction of an annual pollination subsidy is not currently foreseen, the Commission will continue to engage with stakeholders and Member States to develop effective strategies for the sector.
